newsitem.title: POLAND: Zloty holds at resistance as foreigners quiet.
newsitem.headline: Zloty holds at resistance as foreigners quiet.

text.p: The zloty remained pitted against strong resistance at 2.5 percent from the parity rate in early trade with market aware that any gains could set off a central bank currency-buying intervention, dealers said.

They said that foreign investors, whose purchases of Polish treasuries put upward pressure on the zloty over the last two weeks, have already carried out most forex transactions ahead of Monday's 1.3 billion zloty primary T-bill tender.
"Most foreigner forex deals have already gone through the market, but an intervention later in the day can't be ruled out," Witold Wozniak, forex dealer at Deutsche Bank Polska SA.
At 0815 GMT the zloty stood at 2.50/2.48 percent from the trading band centre, slightly weaker from opening at 2.54/2.49 percent and just up from Friday's close at 2.47/2.45 pct.
It was at 3.1610/13 to the dollar, flat from opening's 3.1605/15 and at 1.8262/67 to the mark, down from 1.8250/60.

Dealers said the local market was closely eyeing dollar/mark trends on world markets after the U.S. currency soared to a three-year high at 1.7389 marks following a communique by the G7. The dollar now stands at 1.7310 marks.
Money market rates rose as some banks searched for cash ahead of Tuesday -- the last day of the April reserve period.
At 0830 GMT the zloty overnight rates rose to 15.0/20.0 percent from 13.0/17.0 percent at 0630 GMT, while tomorrow/next were at 17.0/21.0 percent, up from 15.0/18.0.
Dealers said however that there were still more lenders on the market and that rates should remain well below the National Bank of Poland main 14-day drainage rate of 22.15 percent.

Dealers said the NBP's late Friday announcement that from April 30 it would increase the obligatory reserve requirement on zloty term deposits by two points to 11 percent and by one point to five percent on all foreign currency deposits, could put upward pressure on NBP-bill yields.

"There are signals from the secondary market that the reserve increase could push NBP-bill yields higher...and they could have a longer-term echo effect on T-bills," said Robert Gluch, dealer at ING Bank in Warsaw.

Dealers said the NBP's move was aimed at further cooling domestic demand and credit action after Poland's gross domestic product GDP) grew as much as year-on-year eight percent in the first quarter of 1997 after growing by six percent last year.
They said the increase would not support yields at Monday's T-bill auction, where foreign investor bids were expected to push the benchmark 52-week yield down to 21.50-60 percent.
